episodes.title: Episode 02: A sharper ruler, and what it measured
notes: Arms A and B both ~62% vs c2; 300 kingdoms can't resolve 1-3 point differences
Decision bank: 240 positions, every option x 2,048 rollouts = truth; regret per decision
c2 alone 0.88 pts; today's teacher 0.57; value-net leaves floor at ~0.48-0.50 (bias)
320 draws (3 processes) + gate margin 0.01, z 1: 0.38 -- the advisor now uses this gate
Card-choice teacher +4.9 pts [-0.7, +10.1] over today's after 72 kingdoms; candidate arm H running
transcript: This morning I started two matches side by side. One was today's teacher. The other stopped its playouts early and asked the network who was winning. By lunch, both were winning about sixty two percent of their games against plain c2. That confirms the teacher is strong. But it also showed me a problem with how I was measuring.

The difference between the two was less than one point. And after sixty kingdoms, the uncertainty was ten points either way. Even three hundred kingdoms would only get that down to about four. The changes I am testing are worth one to three points. So a whole match, which takes ten hours, could not tell them apart. I stopped the early-stopping match, and the plan for four more matches went with it.

Instead, I built a sharper ruler. I took two hundred and forty real decisions from c2's own games. There are buys, and there are action plays. For each one, I played every legal option to the end of the game two thousand and forty eight times. That is the truth, as close as this laptop can get to it. Then I asked each version of the teacher the same questions, three times each, and measured how much win chance its choice gives up compared with the truth. I call that the regret.

Here is what it found. The c2 network on its own gives up almost nine tenths of a point of win chance per decision. That sounds small, but there are about thirty five real decisions per game. Today's teacher brings it down to just under six tenths.

Stopping early did not hold up. With six hundred and forty playouts it was a little better than today's teacher. But with sixteen hundred it was no better at all. It hit a floor at about half a point. That floor is the network's own misjudgement of positions. More playouts cannot fix a biased judge. So I have dropped that idea.
Full playouts kept improving. With three hundred and twenty draws, which is what three processes give the advisor, the regret fell to under half a point.

And the biggest surprise was the override rule. Today the teacher only overrides when its gain is bigger than two standard errors. That turns out to be too careful. With one standard error, the regret fell at every budget I tried. With three hundred and twenty draws it reached about four tenths of a point. That is less than half of what c2 gives up on its own. I checked that this was not one lucky setting. The whole table is smooth around it. I have already changed the advisor to use the new rule.

One more thing looks promising. The teacher now also checks the card choices inside your actions. That means what to gain with a Workshop or an Artisan, what to trash with a Remodel, and what to play twice with a Throne Room. In the match, that version is ahead of today's teacher by about five points after seventy kingdoms. That is not certain yet. The uncertainty still reaches just below zero.

So, next. One match now plays the full candidate. It uses three hundred and twenty draws, the new override rule, and the card choices. It plays the same kingdoms as today's teacher, so the two can be compared game by game. If it holds up, it goes into the advisor for your next session.

episodes.title: Episode 01: Four days to sharpen the teacher
notes: Goal: a stronger advisor teacher inside the same 3-second budget, 4 days
Value-net leaves after 4 turns: 5x cheaper, within-position correlation 0.87 with full rollouts
3 processes pool their draws exactly: 2.4x draws per second on an idle laptop
Arms running: today's teacher (128 draws) vs leaves (640 draws), 300 kingdoms x 2 seats vs c2
Advisor now uses c2 for its own suggestion; matches pause while you play
transcript: You asked for four days of work on the strongest thing the advisor has. That is the teacher. When you reach a buy or an action in your Steam game, the advisor shows the network's pick at once. Then the teacher checks it. It copies the game and deals the cards it cannot see at random. Then it lets the c2 network play both sides to the very end, once for every option, on the same deal. It repeats that about a hundred and twenty eight times. The option that wins most often is the advice. In earlier matches this teacher beat plain c2 about sixty percent of the time. No network on its own has come close to that.
So this project does not train a new network. The last project tried that for a day and a half, and c2 did not get any better. Instead, I am working on the search itself.

The teacher has one real enemy, and that is noise. It gets three seconds per question, on a laptop that is also running the game. A game played to the end takes about one and a half milliseconds. So three seconds buys roughly eighteen hundred games, shared by up to eleven options. With that many, each option's win rate is only known to about four points either way. Many real decisions are closer than that.
I am trying four ways to beat the noise.

The first is to stop early. Most of the luck in a game played to the end comes from turns far away from the decision. So the teacher can stop four turns later and ask the network how likely it is to win from there. I measured it this morning. Stopping after four turns is five times cheaper. And it ranks the options in a position almost the same way as full games do. The correlation is zero point eight seven. The risk is that the network's own guess is wrong in a way that favours some options. Only a match can tell.

The second is to spend the games where the decision is. Today, a hopeless option gets as many games as the two real contenders. With successive halving, the worse half of the options is dropped after each round, and the last two share what is left.

The third is more cores. The teacher used one. Now three processes answer the same question on different deals, and their answers are merged exactly. On a quiet laptop that gives two point four times as many games in the same second.
The fourth is the override rule. Today the teacher only overrides when the gain is above two points and above two standard errors. With less noise, that rule may be too careful.

Right now, two match arms are running side by side on the same three hundred fresh kingdoms, both seats each. One is today's teacher. The other stops early and plays five times as many games in about the same time. Each game takes about four minutes, so the first real answer comes this evening.

Two more things changed for you. The advisor's own suggestion now comes from c2, the same network the teacher plays with, instead of the older one. And the matches now pause by themselves when the game or the advisor is running, so your games get the whole laptop.
Next time, I will have the first head to head numbers.
